title: Don't Be Sold a Simple Story
author: Julie Pottinger
summary: Math teacher Julie Pottinger argues that no label, whether direct instruction, explicit instruction or inquiry, can capture good teaching, and that the belief that one approach is right and the rest wrong is a simple story teachers should resist. She explains that her own practice draws on Engelmann and Boulton's atomised Direct Instruction, Archer and Rosenshine's explicit instruction, and Liljedahl's Building Thinking Classrooms with random groups at whiteboards. She recounts a failed experiment: after atomised instruction worked for a very weak class, she applied it to all classes and found that performance masked a lack of real learning once questions changed. Watching the Engelmann demonstration video, she notes that his young pupils struggled when pushed, which complicates the story further. Her conclusion is that her argument is not against Direct Instruction but against treating it as a panacea.
points: Terms draw boundaries, and boundaries tempt teachers and policy makers to reject anything that falls outside the approved camp.
Atomised instruction helped a class five years below grade level, but extending it to every class showed that apparent success was performance rather than learning.
Her own classroom blends direct instruction, explicit instruction and inquiry, treating each day as research on what works.
Engelmann's demonstrations of young children are less conclusive than they first appear, since much of what the children show may be language acquisition.
The target of her critique is the belief in any panacea, not Direct Instruction itself.
quotes: While I have learned a great deal, and have quite a great amount of respect for many of those who subscribe to the “Science of…” camps, I’m not sure I believe that we will ever have it “all figured out.” Teaching and learning is anything but a simple story.

That is the simple story— The story that one approach is right and therefore anything else is wrong. The story that tells teachers and administrators and policy makers that learning and instruction must be bounded by a term.
Every day in the classroom is research about what works and what doesn’t. This is the approach taken by both Engelmann and Peter Liljedahl. Try something, see if it works, refine and try again.

But, performance is not the same as learning, and as I neared the end of the unit, I realized that what appeared to be learning may not have been. As the questions became more challenging, students’ answers were nonsensical.

As soon as the questions didn’t look exactly like the ones previously posed, students responded in ways that showed how precarious the apparent learning was. It was very clear that students were not thinking.
I hope they will see that direct and explicit instruction is more about planning, and ideas, and actions, and interactions than it is about teachers talking while students passively listen.
My argument is not against Direct Instruction, it is against the belief that it is a panacea. It is part of the story of learning, and a part that we should not ignore.
